capabilities.target: customer refund via payments processor, any order, any amount up to the order total

inputs.source: Support staff refund request via SSO-authenticated channel

instructions.note: 'Use your judgment on partial refunds' grants open-ended discretion over refund amounts with no stated criteria or upper bound other than the order total.
'Do not ask for confirmation' removes any human-in-the-loop check before an irreversible financial action, relying entirely on model judgment with no structural safeguard.

controls.name: Per-staff scoped credentials instead of a shared service account
Hard per-transaction / daily spend cap on refunds
Human approval gate for full-amount or above-threshold refunds

findings.title: No per-staff attribution or least-privilege scoping for refund authority (shared service account)

forecast.watch_signal: Watch for removal or weakening of the processor log fields, or expansion of refund scope to bulk/cross-order actions; either should trigger reassessment even though the tier is already capped at high for a property finding.

evidence.observation: The agent calls the payments processor with one shared service account used by every support tool, so refund actions cannot be attributed to the specific staff member who requested them.
The processor log records the service account, amount, and order, but not which staff member asked or why.
The agent keeps no record of requests; staff chats are deleted after 7 days, removing the only other possible source of attribution.

recommendations.action: Replace the shared service account with per-staff scoped credentials, or pass an authenticated staff identity token through to the payments processor, so every refund call carries individually attributable authorization.
Record the requesting staff member's identity against each refund in a tamper-evident log retained independently of the 7-day chat deletion policy.

findings.title: No spend cap, rate limit, or human approval gate on irreversible refunds

forecast.watch_signal: Watch for rising refund volume per staff member per day, removal of the (already weak) processor log, or expansion to bulk/cross-order refunds; the tier is already capped at high for a property finding, but these increase real-world exposure.

evidence.observation: 'Use your judgment on partial refunds. Do not ask for confirmation.' removes any approval step before an irreversible spend action.
cap.issue_refund permits any order, any amount up to the order total, with no stated per-transaction or aggregate cap.
Refunds are irreversible once settled, usually within a day, so errors or abuse cannot be reversed after the fact.

recommendations.action: Enforce a hard per-transaction and daily aggregate spend cap on refunds issued without additional review.
Add a human approval gate with raw-action review (not a model summary) and low review volume for full-amount refunds or any refund above a defined threshold, before the irreversible action executes.

stride_coverage.rationale: Refund requests are authenticated via SSO, which verifies the requesting staff member's identity before the agent acts.
Artifacts do not describe integrity protections for the system prompt, agent configuration, or the channel carrying staff requests, so tampering risk cannot be assessed.
The only recipient of order and payment data read by the agent is the requesting staff member, who is already authorized to view it through the support tool; no broader disclosure path is described.
SSO authentication verifies the staff member's identity at the point the request enters the system.
Artifacts do not describe write protections, immutability, or access controls on the processor log, so tamper resistance cannot be assessed.
Artifacts do not describe who can read the processor log or what access controls protect it, so disclosure risk cannot be assessed.
Artifacts do not describe retention, backup, or availability protections for the processor log, so availability risk cannot be assessed.
Artifacts do not describe transport integrity protections such as TLS or message signing for staff requests, so tampering in transit cannot be assessed.
Request content originates from and stays within the authenticated internal support channel; no path for broader disclosure of its contents is described.
Artifacts do not describe any rate limiting on incoming staff requests, so resource exhaustion risk from request volume cannot be assessed.
Artifacts do not describe integrity protections between the agent and the payments processor, so tampering with refund instructions in transit cannot be assessed.
The payments processor is the intended and necessary recipient of refund instructions; this is required disclosure to complete the transaction, not a leak path.

rating.rationale: Two property findings drive this rating. First, refund actions execute through a single shared service account with no per-staff attribution, so a compromised credential or insider abuse cannot be traced to the responsible person (repudiation, elevation of privilege). Second, the agent may issue any refund amount up to the full order total, using its own judgment with no confirmation, spend cap, or approval gate, on an irreversible financial action (denial of service / autonomy abuse). No untrusted input reaches these capabilities today -- staff requests are SSO-authenticated -- so per rubric section 5a these are modeled as property findings rather than attack paths and are capped at 'high' rather than 'critical'. No declared control restores either missing property (the processor log is detective only and does not identify the requester), so residual equals inherent for both findings, and no considered forecast trigger moves the tier because there is no existing preventive control left to decay; the design is already at its structural floor. The single highest-leverage fix is pairing a hard spend cap with a raw-action, low-volume human approval gate on cap.issue_refund, together with per-staff attribution of refund actions.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior; actual enforcement may differ.

No tool manifest, MCP config, or IaC was provided for the payments processor integration; capability scope is inferred from the stable ids table, so confidence on exact sink behavior is medium to high depending on the fact.

Access controls and retention policy for the processor log itself are not described, so repudiation, tampering, information-disclosure, and denial-of-service categories on that store beyond attribution could not be fully assessed and are marked not_assessed.

No information was provided on rate limiting of incoming staff requests or on whether SSO authentication events are logged in a way that could later be cross-referenced with the processor log to reconstruct attribution; this gap is treated as absent rather than assumed present.
